title: The most beautiful names
hook: to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call on Him by them (7:180)

segments.voice: Yesterday, camp four closed with hifz: seventy-five days from An-Nas back to An-Naba'. Your line was the ones every child knows. Today, camp five begins.

Abdullah. Abdul-Rahman. Abdul-Karim. Abdul-Aziz. Abdul-Latif. Each of these names starts the same way, 'abd, servant of, and then comes a name of God. Servant of the Merciful. Servant of the Generous. Servant of the Mighty. Servant of the Gentle. A person can carry a name of God inside their own name for a lifetime and hardly notice it's there. So saying hi to an Abdul-Rahman means saying one of the most beautiful names out loud. Camp five is called further in, and it begins with the names.
screen: `ABDULLAH, ABDUL-RAHMAN, ABDUL-KARIM.` → `SERVANT OF A NAME.` → `CAMP FIVE: FURTHER IN.`

segments.voice: The phrase comes straight from the Qur'an. Pickthall's translation of Surah al-A'raf: Allah's are the fairest names. Invoke Him by them. Asma' is the plural of ism, name. Husna is the feminine form of ahsan: most beautiful, best, finest. The phrase comes back in other surahs too: at the end of al-Hashr, in Ta Ha, and in al-Isra', where people are told they may call on Allah or call on the Most Merciful; whichever they call, His are the most beautiful names. Why names, and not a description? Muslim teaching holds that in this life Allah can't be seen, pictured or fully understood, but He can be known through what He has told people about Himself. Each name is like a window: you can't see the whole house through one window, but you can see something true. The Merciful. The Living. Peace. The Loving. And notice the verb: invoke Him by them, call on Him by them. The names aren't for a list on a wall. They're for calling. A person who is afraid might call on the Protector. A person who has done wrong calls on the Forgiving. Someone lost calls on the Guide. You've met several already: ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim in every bismillah, al-Wadud, the Loving, in al-Buruj, al-Hayy and al-Qayyum in Ayat al-Kursi. For the next weeks the path takes them one at a time, a first selection, and each one will be a new way to call.
screen: `ASMA' — NAMES. HUSNA — MOST BEAUTIFUL.` · `EACH NAME A WINDOW.` · `NAMES ARE FOR CALLING.` · `THE ONES YOU'VE ALREADY MET.` · then, large: `CALL HIM BY HIS NAMES.`

segments.voice: Look for a name of Allah you already know: ar-Rahman from the bismillah, as-Salam, peace, hidden in the greeting, or al-Wadud, the Loving. Pick one and say it slowly in your mind with each out-breath, noticing what it brings up, a feeling, a memory, a need. If you pray, you can call on Allah by that name, simply: ya Rahman, O Most Merciful; if you don't, just let the name and its meaning sit with you.
Al-asma' al-husna. The most beautiful names: the names by which Allah is known in the Qur'an, given to call on Him by. Today's word.
Your line: call him by his names. Every bismillah already holds two of them. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims call on Allah by the name that fits their need in du'a (ya Rahman, ya Ghafur), often learn the names as children through recited lists, and carry them in personal names like Abdullah and Abdul-Rahman.
